chapter_theme: Verses 81 to 100 count threes under predicates of loss and power: those who sink in craving, who are born yet unborn, who are utter fools or miss the good world, set against the wife, ascetic, king and priest whose keeping of their station brings rain, with the spy and the king's limbs closing the book on rule.

81.reading: The courtesan who lives by offering her shoulders like a public ford, the gambler without decency who looks to the gaming hall every day, and the man who makes bright wealth by taking a premium on money are named three who sink in the sea of craving.
81.nuance: The three are not the customers of vice but those who live by it: the seller of the body, the professional gambler and the money-dealer. வாசி is read here as the premium or discount taken in exchanging or lending money; the word allows other trades, so the third figure is the least certain.

items.claim: the courtesan who lives by giving her shoulders to all comers, like a ford anyone may use, sinks in craving
the graceless gambler who looks to the gaming hall daily sinks in craving
the man who makes fine wealth by taking a premium on money sinks in craving

82.reading: Being called worthy among the worthy at all times, being called close among those who are close, and not saying, even when roused to spring up, what those who will not take it would not accept are named three as the way a good person offers.
82.nuance: The first two are standings given by peers, the third a restraint one keeps oneself, so the verse makes reputation and silence one path. நல்லாள் can be a good person or a good woman; nothing else in the verse points to a woman, so it is read generally.

items.claim: to be called worthy by the worthy themselves belongs to the good person's path
to be called intimate by those one is intimate with belongs to that path
not speaking, even when provoked, what the unreceptive will not receive belongs to that path

83.reading: A great heap of salt is gone if water soaks it, the rich shoot of friendship is gone if a lie is dealt, and the upright are like rain; these three are named a way the path of rectitude is kept from being choked.
83.nuance: Two items are images of dissolution and the third an image of giving, and the closing predicate (செப்பநெறி தூரா ஆறு) has to cover both; it is read as lessons that keep the straight path open, which is a guess at how the list holds together.

items.claim: a great heap of salt vanishes once water soaks into it
the thriving shoot of friendship vanishes once falsehood is dealt in it
the upright are like rain, giving to all

84.reading: A tank whose inlet is not well made, an infant that has not drunk its fill at its mother's breast, and people of a long line who lack the excellence of learning are named three joined to poverty.
84.nuance: All three fail to take in what should fill them: water, milk, learning. சேய்மரபில் is read as 'in a long or distant line'; it could instead mean those of a far-off or lesser descent, which would change who the third item faults.

items.claim: a tank whose mouth is badly made is poor
an infant not fed full at its mother's breast is poor
people of a long line who lack excellence in learning are poor

85.reading: Being of a kind that people scorn, a sharpness that does not forget a secret once heard, and the perception that reports the hidden matter without fail are named the three qualities of a spy worth considering.
85.nuance: The first quality is not a virtue but a cover: to belong to a despised kind is to be overlooked, and the verse counts it among qualities on the same footing as memory and judgment.

items.claim: being of a kind people look down on is a spy's quality
a sharpness that never forgets the secret it has heard is a spy's quality
the discernment to report the hidden matter without gaps is a spy's quality

86.reading: The loosening and ending of the great tie of love, letting go of the great raft of chastity out of desire, and the loss of friendship's gracious nature are named three as an enmity that brings fault.
86.nuance: The three are bonds (a tie, a raft, a nature) and their breaking is called an enmity, as if the broken bond turns into an enemy. Whose chastity is let go is not said: it can be a wife's lapse or, as verse 97 suggests, a husband's casting off a chaste wife for another desire.

items.claim: the great bond of love coming loose and ending is an enmity that brings fault
letting the great raft of chastity go out of desire is an enmity that brings fault
friendship losing its gracious quality is an enmity that brings fault

87.reading: One who, without fear, wants to kill, one who goes into a company far from learning, and one who sits idle and lets great wealth dwindle are named three fit to be utter fools.

items.claim: the man who, not afraid of it, wants to kill is an utter fool
the man who enters a company remote from learning is an utter fool
the man who sits still and lets a great store of wealth shrink is an utter fool

88.reading: The way one suffers when disease eats at him, the way great Death, never abating, consumes life, and wealth tied to one moving on without worth are named three ways that unsettle the standing of the raft.
88.nuance: The raft (புணை) is most likely the body or the life it carries. The third item is the hardest: பிணைசெல்வம் may be wealth bound to one, or pledged wealth, and மாண்பின்று இயங்கல் may mean it passes away without dignity; the reading given is one of several the words allow. The count word is fused by sandhi with the third item (இயங்கலிவை மூன்றும்), so only மூன்றும் is given as written.

items.claim: the suffering when disease devours one shakes the raft
unrelenting Death eating up life shakes the raft
bound wealth moving on without worth shakes the raft

89.reading: One who gives grace no room in his heart, one who buries wealth without enjoying it, and one who oversteps and speaks hurtful words are named three who, though born, are as if never born.

items.claim: the man who gives grace no shelter in his heart is unborn though born
the man who buries his wealth and does not enjoy it is unborn though born
the man who exceeds measure and can speak painful words is unborn though born

90.reading: The verse names earning wealth for the sake of giving, learning the great books so as to join the path of dharma, and speaking words always with grace as three ways not to reach the world of darkness.
90.nuance: This is one of the few verses in the book in the imperative (செய்க, சொல்லுக); each item gives a purpose to a means, wealth for giving and books for dharma, so earning and study are judged by their end.

items.claim: making wealth for the sake of giving keeps one from the dark world
studying the great books to join dharma's path keeps one from the dark world
speaking every word with grace keeps one from the dark world

91.reading: Speaking heedlessly at the moment of gain, saying at the end 'we have lost our life', and feeling shame when a blemish comes and one's own body withers are named three signs of the body that does not last.
91.nuance: The predicate can mean signs that the body is passing (marks of approaching death) or the marks of one who lives as if the body were not passing; the first item, heedless speech at a gain, fits the second sense better, the second and third the first.

items.claim: speaking forgetfully at a time of gain is a sign of the passing body
saying at the end that one has lost one's life is a sign of the passing body
shame when a blemish appears and one's body withers is a sign of the passing body

92.reading: One not born in an excellent family line, the wretch who understands not a single letter, and one who always delights in excessive speech are named three who, though born, are as if never born.
92.nuance: விழுத்திணை is read as a high birth-group or lineage (திணை as kind or clan), which makes the first item a rule about birth ranked with two faults of learning and speech. If திணை is read as conduct, the item would fault character instead; the birth reading is the plainer one.

norm.note: a birth-rank judgment of the period: not being born in an excellent line is counted with illiteracy as making a life void

items.claim: the man not born into an excellent line is as if unborn
the poor wretch who knows not one letter is as if unborn
the man who loves speaking beyond measure is as if unborn

93.reading: A world that passes away in darkness, anger that speaks without knowing anything, and desire that sets love on things of no worth are named three that belong to a creature living in folly.
93.nuance: The three are the familiar triad of delusion, anger and desire, each given by what it does: delusion as a world gone dark, anger as speech without knowledge, desire as love for what is not wealth.

items.claim: a life passing in darkness belongs to the fool
anger that speaks knowing nothing belongs to the fool
desire that fixes love on things of no worth belongs to the fool

94.reading: One who seeks intimacy of desire with those who bear no friendship, the fool who neglects guarding his woman, and one who speaks words that slip from good character are named three who do not hold to right conduct.
94.nuance: பெண்பாலைக் காப்பிகழும் is read as a man neglecting to guard the woman of his house; the verse counts this as his own lapse of conduct.

norm.note: a gender norm of the period: a man's guarding of the woman of his house is treated as part of his conduct

items.claim: the man who courts intimacy with the unfriendly does not keep conduct
the fool who neglects guarding his woman does not keep conduct
the man who speaks words that fall from good character does not keep conduct

95.reading: The disease of hunger that eats until wisdom fails, desire that arises so that self-restraint fails, and anger that cannot bear the hot words of enemies are named three as an army that drives out good deeds.
95.nuance: Hunger, a bodily need, stands in one army with two passions. Line 2 is read as செறிவு அழுங்க, restraint perishing, which the printed text's செறிவழங்க only half shows.

items.claim: the hunger-sickness that eats until wisdom fails drives out good deeds
desire that rises to undo restraint drives out good deeds
anger unable to bear enemies' harsh words drives out good deeds

96.reading: The wife who knows her husband's mind, the ascetic who carries out what he has undertaken, and the king who shuns cruelty and does good are named three at whose word 'rain' the rain falls.
96.domain_note: a wife, an ascetic and a king, one each
96.nuance: The wife's power is defined by her husband's intention, the ascetic's by his vows, the king's by his justice: each keeps the line of a station. Line 1 prints குறிப்பறிவான், a masculine form, for the wife.

norm.note: a gender norm of the period: a wife's merit is defined by knowing and following her husband's mind

items.claim: the wife who knows her husband's wish commands the rain
the ascetic who performs what he has taken on commands the rain
the king who turns from cruelty and does good commands the rain

97.reading: Refusing the command of the five elders, false dealing within a whole and eager friendship, and abandoning the chaste wife settled in one's heart are named three as the acts of those without goodness.
97.nuance: நற்புடையிலாளர் is an unusual form, read as 'those who lack goodness'.

items.claim: refusing the five elders' command is the act of the graceless
dealing falsely in a full friendship is the act of the graceless
forsaking a chaste wife dear to one's heart is the act of the graceless

98.reading: The fire-priests living with dharma in mind, the fiercely angry king keeping to the path of just rule, and the wife going the way of her husband are named three as the seed of the month's three rains.
98.domain_note: priests, the king and a wife, one each
98.nuance: செந்தீ முதல்வர், those foremost at the red fire, names the fire-tending priests by their rite; the verse sets their dharma first and makes a priestly order, a royal order and a wife's obedience joint causes of the rains.

norm.note: norms of the period: the fire-priests' dharma and the wife's following of her husband are stated as causes of rain

items.claim: the fire-priests living mindful of dharma are a seed of the rains
the fierce king keeping to just rule is a seed of the rains
the wife going her husband's way is a seed of the rains

99.reading: Living after forsaking the learned, the fool who acts on whatever he desires, and the babbler who does wrong unchecked are named three who will not reach the good world.

items.claim: living with the learned cast off bars one from the good world
the fool who does as he pleases does not reach the good world
the babbler who does wrong without restraint does not reach the good world

100.reading: An army full of loyalty, a fortress that fears nothing however many gather against it, and great treasure laid up beyond counting are named three as the limbs of kings who rule the earth.

items.claim: an army full of loyalty is a limb of kingship
a walled fort that fears no numbers is a limb of kingship
a stored treasure that counting cannot exhaust is a limb of kingship

links.note: Kural 920 names double-minded women, liquor and dice as the company of those Fortune has left; Thirikadugam names the courtesan, the gambler and the money-dealer themselves as sinking in craving.
links.teaches: The couplet ruins the customer of these trades; the verse drowns the traders too, so vice is shown to consume both sides of the bargain.
links.list_adds: It replaces liquor with the money-dealer, so all three are people who live by others' wants and are judged by their own greed rather than by the harm they do.

links.note: Naladiyar 371 says a harlot's love ends when the hand is empty, like a lamp without oil; Thirikadugam says the courtesan herself sinks in the sea of craving.
links.teaches: The quatrain explains why her love fails (it follows money); the verse names the cost to her, so the same greed that makes her love brief also drowns her.
links.list_adds: It sets the courtesan beside the gambler and the usurer, making her one of three money-trades rather than a figure of false love.

links.note: Kural 720 says holding forth before those not of one's group is nectar spilled in a drain; Thirikadugam counts not saying what the unreceptive will not accept, even when provoked, as part of a good person's path.
links.teaches: The couplet gives the reason for silence before the wrong audience as waste; the verse makes that silence a mark of standing, kept even under provocation.
links.list_adds: It sets restraint before the unreceptive beside being acknowledged by the worthy and the intimate, so the silence counts as one of three signs of a good person's standing.

links.note: Kural 112 says the wealth of the upright does not decay and supports those after them; Thirikadugam says the upright are like rain.
links.teaches: The couplet keeps the yield of rectitude within the upright man's line; the rain image sends it outward to all, so rectitude is shown both lasting and shared.
links.list_adds: It sets the upright against two images of dissolution (salt in water, friendship under a lie), so rectitude stands as the one thing in the list that gives instead of melting.

links.note: Verse 15 says the man who lives by lies is not to be befriended; verse 83 says a lie dissolves friendship's thriving shoot as water dissolves salt.
links.teaches: One verse keeps the liar out of friendship at the start and the other shows a lie undoing friendship already grown, so the book makes falsehood fatal to friendship at both ends.

links.note: Kural 408 says wealth in the hands of the unlearned is more painful than poverty among the good; Thirikadugam counts the unlearned among those already joined to poverty.
links.teaches: Read together, the unlearned rich man is poor twice: the couplet makes his coin a grief and the verse makes him poor in what he never took in, so poverty is a lack of intake as well as of money.
links.list_adds: It sets the unlearned with a tank whose inlet fails and an infant not fed full, so lack of learning becomes a vessel that cannot fill, a kind of poverty the couplet does not name.

links.note: Kural 585 asks a spy to have an appearance that raises no suspicion and to let nothing spill; Thirikadugam asks him to be of a despised kind, to forget nothing he hears and to report the hidden matter fully.
links.teaches: The verse makes the couplet's unsuspected look specific: contempt is the cover, because people do not guard their words before the despised, and it adds the report that the couplet's silence serves.
links.list_adds: It pairs the disguise with memory and accurate report, so the spy's work is a sequence (hear unseen, keep, deliver) where the couplet gives only concealment.

links.note: Verse 9 lists what utter fools love, beginning with moving away from the company of the great; verse 87 lists who are utter fools, including the man who enters a company remote from learning.
links.teaches: The two verses share the predicate முழுமக்கள் and both define the utter fool by the company he leaves or joins, so the book makes the choice of company the first test of folly.

links.note: Kural 1001 says one who stores great wealth and does not eat it is dead; Thirikadugam says one who buries wealth without enjoying it is born yet unborn.
links.teaches: The couplet counts the hoarder dead at the end; the verse counts him never born, so between them the hoarder's life is cancelled at both ends.
links.list_adds: It sets the hoarder beside the graceless heart and the overreaching harsh tongue, so hoarding becomes one of three refusals (of grace, of use, of measure in speech) that unmake a birth.

links.note: Naladiyar 273 says the fool who neither enjoys nor gives his wealth is mocked by that wealth and by the world's compassion; Thirikadugam counts the graceless heart and the buried wealth as two separate items.
links.teaches: The quatrain fuses the failure of compassion and the failure to use wealth into one mockery; the verse separates them, showing the Naladiyar's single fault as two distinct ways of being unborn.
links.list_adds: It counts the graceless heart and the buried treasure as two items with harsh speech as a third, where the quatrain treats compassion only as the hoarder's judge.

links.note: Kural 243 says those whose hearts are joined with grace do not enter the painful world of darkness; Thirikadugam names gracious speech, earning for giving and study for dharma as three ways not to reach the dark world.
links.teaches: The couplet locates the escape from the dark world in the heart; the verse carries grace into speech and adds two practical means, so the escape becomes a matter of how one talks, earns and studies.
links.list_adds: It turns grace from a state of heart into a manner of speaking and sets it beside wealth and learning used for their ends, so three daily practices replace one inner condition.

links.note: Verse 89 names the graceless heart, buried wealth and harsh speech as unmaking a birth; verse 90 names earning for giving, studying for dharma and gracious speech as the way past the dark world.
links.teaches: Verse 90 answers 89 item for item on wealth and speech, so the book shows the same two goods (wealth, words) as either cancelling a life or saving it, depending on use.

links.note: Kural 972 says birth is alike for all and distinction differs by what one does; Thirikadugam counts the man not born in an excellent line as born yet unborn, on the reading that விழுத்திணை is a high birth-group, not conduct.
links.teaches: The ethics group splits on whether lineage can void a life: the couplet places worth in work, the verse places a birth condition beside illiteracy and boasting as equal disqualifiers.
links.list_adds: It puts low birth in one row with two faults one can mend, so birth is treated as a fault of the same kind as conduct, which the couplet denies.

links.note: Verses 89 and 92 share the predicate 'born yet unborn'; 89 lists failures of grace, use of wealth and speech, 92 failures of birth, letters and speech.
links.teaches: Both lists include a fault of speech, but 92 adds birth and literacy where 89 has grace and wealth, so the book's 'unborn' joins conditions one chooses with a condition one cannot.

links.note: Kural 410 says others stand to those learned in the shining books as beasts stand to people; Thirikadugam says one who knows not a single letter is born yet unborn.
links.teaches: The couplet lowers the unlearned to beasts; the verse goes further and denies them birth, and sets the bar at one letter rather than at the great books.
links.list_adds: It sets the illiterate beside the low-born and the boaster, pairing a lack of letters with a lack of lineage as one kind of void life.

links.note: Kural 360 says pain perishes when the very names of desire, anger and confusion perish; Thirikadugam names a world passing in darkness, anger that speaks without knowledge and desire for worthless things as what belongs to a creature in folly.
links.teaches: The verse gives each of the Kural's three its mark (confusion as a darkened world, anger as speech without knowledge, desire as love of the worthless), so the couplet's bare names gain definitions.
links.list_adds: It describes each member of the triad by its effect and assigns all three to the fool, where the couplet only names them as what must be destroyed.

links.note: Kural 57 asks what use guarding women by confinement is and makes their own steadfastness the chief guard; Thirikadugam counts the man who neglects guarding his woman among those without right conduct.
links.teaches: The couplet moves a woman's guard inside her; the verse keeps an outer guarding as the husband's duty and faults him for neglecting it, so the group holds both views of where the guard lies.
links.list_adds: It ranks neglect of guarding a woman with courting the unfriendly and faulty speech, so it becomes a lapse of the man's own conduct, not a question of the woman's virtue.

links.note: Kural 225 says the strength of the strong is enduring hunger, though it ranks below relieving others' hunger; Thirikadugam counts hunger that eats away wisdom as one of three forces that drive out good deeds.
links.teaches: The verse shows why enduring hunger is a strength in the couplet: hunger is an army against merit, so bearing it is holding a line, and relieving it removes the enemy itself.
links.list_adds: It sets hunger in one army with desire and anger, so a bodily need is ranked as a moral enemy beside two passions.

links.note: Verse 93 gives anger and desire to the creature in folly; verse 95 sets anger and desire beside hunger as an army that drives out good deeds.
links.teaches: Read together, the book treats anger and desire both as the condition of folly and as the force that removes merit, and swaps the third member, delusion, for hunger.

links.note: Kural 55 says that if the wife who rises worshipping her husband says 'rain', it rains; Thirikadugam gives the same rain-command to the wife who knows her husband's mind, the ascetic true to his undertaking and the king who shuns cruelty.
links.teaches: The Kural gives the power over rain to the wife alone; the verse shares it with the ascetic and the king, so it becomes the reward of anyone who keeps the line of his station.
links.list_adds: It names three holders of the rain-power from household, renunciation and rule, turning the couplet's single wonder into a rule about keeping one's station.

links.note: Acharakkovai 16 names the king, teacher, mother, father and elder brother as the peerless elders to be worshipped as gods; Thirikadugam counts refusing the five elders' command as the act of those without goodness.
links.teaches: Acharakkovai supplies who the ஐங்குரவர் are and the positive rule; Thirikadugam names the breach and ranks it with lying in friendship and casting off a chaste wife, setting obedience to elders in one ethic with loyalty to friend and wife.

links.note: Verse 86 calls letting go of the raft of chastity and the loss of friendship's grace an enmity; verse 97 names forsaking a chaste wife and false dealing in friendship as acts of the graceless.
links.teaches: Verse 97 names plainly the husband's act of forsaking a chaste wife beside a breach of friendship, which supports reading 86's letting go of chastity as his act rather than hers.

links.note: Verse 96 gives the rain-command to the wife, the ascetic and the king; verse 98 makes the fire-priests, the just king and the obedient wife the seed of the month's three rains.
links.teaches: The pair shows the book's rain list is fixed on king and wife but varies its third member between ascetic and fire-priest, and moves from command to seed, from a single word to a monthly cause.

links.note: Kural 560 says that if the guardian does not guard, the cows' yield fails and the men of six duties forget their books; Thirikadugam sets the fire-priests' dharma and the king's just rule side by side as seeds of rain.
links.teaches: The couplet makes priestly learning depend on the king's protection; the verse makes priest, king and wife coequal causes of the rains, flattening the Kural's order of dependence into a joint one.
links.list_adds: It adds the wife who follows her husband as a third cause beside priest and king, joining the household to the ritual and royal orders as one seed of rain.

links.note: Verse 90 names giving, study for dharma and gracious speech as the way past the dark world; verse 99 names forsaking the learned, self-will and unchecked wrongdoing as barring the good world.
links.teaches: Study is on one list and the abandonment of the learned on the other, so the book makes learning the hinge between the dark world and the good one.

links.note: Kural 381 names six limbs of a king (army, people, resources, ministers, allies, fort); Thirikadugam names three: a loyal army, a fort fearless of numbers, and uncountable treasure.
links.teaches: The Thirikadugam's king needs only the three material limbs and drops people, ministers and allies, a narrower and more martial account of what makes a king than the Kural's.
links.list_adds: It selects three of the six and qualifies each (loyal, fearless, uncountable), so the list sharpens the quality of each limb where the couplet only counts kinds.

links.note: Kural 1134 has the lover say the flood of desire carries off the raft of shame and manliness; Thirikadugam names letting go the great raft of chastity out of desire as an enmity that brings fault.
links.teaches: Both make a virtue the raft that desire tears away, but the love couplet voices it as a lover's helpless loss while the ethics verse judges the same release as a culpable fault.
links.list_adds: It sets the abandoned raft of chastity beside a loosened bond of love and friendship's lost grace, so the release becomes one of three broken bonds that turn into enmity.

links.note: Naladiyar 52 says the best reflect on impermanence, disease, old age and death and do their own work; Thirikadugam names disease eating one, Death consuming life and wealth passing without worth as what unsettles the raft.
links.teaches: The quatrain draws the conclusion, do your own work now, while the verse shows what that work is threatened by, so the pair gives both the danger and the answer to it.
links.list_adds: It adds the passing of wealth to disease and Death as a third force shaking the raft, so loss of goods is ranked with bodily ruin where the quatrain counts only the body's fates.

links.note: Kural 539 says to think of those ruined by negligence when one is swollen with joy; Thirikadugam counts speaking heedlessly at a time of gain as a sign of the body that does not last.
links.teaches: The couplet treats elated negligence as a danger to be remedied by memory, while the verse reads the same heedless word as a mark of mortality, so forgetting at a gain is shown to be forgetting that one will die.
links.list_adds: It sets heedless speech at a gain beside the cry at the end and shame at a withering body, so negligence is ranked with dying itself as a sign of a perishable life rather than as a tactical fault.

source_issues: 95: the verse is printed without a number and is numbered 95 by its place after 94.
95 line 2: the source prints செறிவழங்கத்; tamilvu has செறிவு அழுங்கத், which the reading follows.
96 line 1: குறிப்பறிவான் is a masculine form attached to பெண்டாட்டி; a feminine form would be expected.
96 line 3: the misprint சொய்வான் was repaired to செய்வான், as tamilvu; the reading differs from the site.
100 line 4: மேந்தர்க்கு is most likely a misprint for வேந்தர்க்கு.
89 line 3: இறந்து இன்னா is printed with a space and no sandhi, unlike the rest of the text.
88 line 3: இயங்கலிவை fuses the end of the third item with the count word இவை; the item and count word are given as the text runs.
